2.	If so, who is the acting head, what is his staff, what duties do they perform and what are their respective salaries and other allowances ?

6.	Has Canada made representations to Eire or to the government of Britain requesting the use of Irish ports and bases as a protection to Canadian and empire shipping against enemy submarines and air bombers?
7.	Have empire ships been sunk, and Canadian and British seamen drowned as a result of the lack of protection by the use of Irish ports?
8.	What has the government done in the matter, or what action will be taken?
[Mr. Jean.3

Questions

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I feel I ought to say a word or two about the questions which the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has asked, and in that connection point out to him and to hon. members of the house that in considering both the placing of questions on the order paper and the replies to be made thereto, it is desirable that we should all have in mind the effect which the questions when asked and when answered may have upon the situation with which the entire British empire is faced at the present time. It is important that we keep in mind particularly the position of the United Kingdom and the government as well as that of our own country in dealing with matters which affect not one part of the empire only, but all parts. If any useful purpose can be served by asking and answering questions, if we can achieve a purpose which will assist the war effort of the British commonwealth, then I think questions might well be asked and should be answered. But if a question is of a character to provoke discussion and is in no way calculated to aid in meeting an existing situation and one which may be very embarrassing, with all due respect I submit that any such question should neither be asked nor answered.
There are one or two questions asked by my hon. friend which I can answer. He asks: "Has Canada a foreign minister or envoy to the Eire republic in Dublin?" I would reply that Canada has no foreign minister in Dublin. There is the office of high commissioner which unhappily, due to the death of the late Mr. John Hall Kelly, is vacant at the present time. At present the acting high commissioner is Mr. E. J. Garland, a former member of this House of Commons. My hon. friend following his first question asks: "If so, who is the acting head, what is his staff, what duties do they perform and what are their respective salaries and other allowances?" I have already given him the name of the acting head. The staff is a small one. It consists of one stenographer, Miss E. O'Malley, grade 3, who receives a salary of $1,560 and an allowance of $250 per annum, and Mr. Chambers, messenger, who receives $465.
I shall have to bring the next question to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). My hon. friend asks: "What trade commissioners or other Canadian officials are in Eire, where are they located, at what cost, and is there duplication of services?" Perhaps this question may be allowed to stand on the order paper to be answered later by my colleague. The hon. member's next question is: "Has the government made any representations to Eire as to the loss of Canadian shipping off Eire ports
by enemy action, resulting from the refusal of Eire of the use of her ports for defence purposes?" To begin with, this question is out of order because it carries with it an implication. It is asked not so much for the purpose of getting information as for the purpose of purporting to give information, which may and probably is wholly incorrect.
The next question asked is: "Has Canada made representations to Eire or to the government of Britain requesting the use of Irish ports and bases as a protection to Canadian and empire shipping against enemy submarines and air bombers?" And next: "Have empire ships been sunk, and Canadian and British seamen drowned as a result of the lack of protection by the use of Irish ports?" What I said a moment ago about a previous question would apply also to these. Then my hon. friend asks: "What has the government done in the matter, or what action will be taken?"
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that to give any replies to these questions, either in the affirmative or in the negative, would serve only to provoke discussion which might prove unfortunate to the relations between Canada and Ireland or create complications as between the United Kingdom and Ireland. I would not wish it to be assumed that the matters which are referred to have not been the subject of careful consideration by representatives of Ireland and our own government. On the other hand, I have no desire to answer questions which might quite unnecessarily occasion further questions or occasion embarrassment in other parts of the empire, with respect to a controversial matter. I think the whole matter is perhaps best left in that position. I am sure that my hon. friend, who is the most loyal of men, will appreciate that it is only because of reasons of great loyalty to the crown that I take the position I do.

I followed the Prime Minister quite closely, but I do not recall that he answered question No. 4, in which the opinion of the government was requested as to whether Eire is considered to be a dominion or a separate republic.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I suppose that is a case of paying your money and taking your choice. I imagine that the United Kingdom would have something to say in regard to that matter as well as ourselves. I do not think we need to go into that particular subject, which is an academic one, at this time.

The British government have answered these questions. I wanted them answered and to know what will be done. There has been great loss of life and shipping
Questions

because of our inability to use these Irish ports, bays and inlets, and the government should make known its stand on the matter. I asked the question on July 10 of last year, as to what our policy was, when the Right Hon. Prime Minister's estimates were under discussion. A statute of Eire, the Irish National and Citizenship Act, declares the United Kingdom to be a foreign power, and the act states that in the event of any war of the United Kingdom, Eire will remain neutral. I do not want this question to stand. We have no foreign policy. The enemy will not let things stand and stop sinking ships. They will continue to destroy our fleet. These ports belong to the empire, not to Eire. I think the house is entitled to know something about the matter, and the country is asking what is being done. Two or three people in my constituency have asked me to take up the matter and have suffered as a result.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
desire this afternoon to make a statement to the house in connection with the decennial census which is due to be taken in June of this year.
In the minds of many persons it has been assumed that the national registration of last summer could take the place of the census.
I wish to make it very clear that the information asked for under the national registration was very different from that required under the census.
The census as it has been developed in this country is far more than a mere counting of heads. I have before me the schedules which will be used. They are eight in number. The one schedule for the national registration of last year contained 16 questions. The census schedule dealing with population statistics contains 39 questions.
There is a general farm schedule comprising 167 main questions and a very great number of subquestions.
There is a special schedule for the fruit and vegetable growers of this country containing 64 questions.
There is a schedule in connection with abandoned or idle farms containing 24 questions.
There is a schedule dealing with those who may be undertaking the production of fruits, vegetables and animals on a small acreage, or to a small value. This schedule has 54 questions.
There is a schedule containing nine questions covering merchandising and service establishments; and to assist in the complete enumeration of those who may be blind, deaf or mute, there is a special schedule containing some seven questions.
For reasons which will be obvious it is proposed in connection with the housing situation to have what is known as a test census. Some twenty-nine main questions will be asked of the owner or occupant of every tenth dwelling.
This brief statement as to the schedules to be used will give hon. members a slight idea of the scope of the information which it is desired to obtain.
It will not be possible to tabulate all the details which it is expected to obtain on these various schedules in a few weeks or even a few months. This means that, if the census were to be postponed for a year, or two years,

Decennial Census
or for that indefinite period "until after the war," particulars regarding housing, the data on abandoned or idle farms, that in connection with the general farm schedule, and other information which would be of infinite value in connection with the problems of demobilization and reestablishment of our soldiers, would not be available when it was required.
The census has been taken in the whole of Canada every tenth year since 1871; and in 1916, 1926 and 1936 there has been a federal census taken in the western provinces. Incidentally, I might point out, 1916 was a war year.
It is necessary that the information obtained be accurately compared with that obtained on previous occasions. If the period elapsing were to be eleven, eleven and a half, or twelve years, or longer, instead of ten years, this accurate comparison would not be possible.
The bureau of statistics has built up an enviable reputation for the information which it is able to provide for businesses of all types. It would be unfortunate if the value of that information were in any way impaired because of the inability of the bureau to make the necessary comparisons which must be made if the true picture of our economic life in Canada is to be obtained.
It is, of course, well known that the decennial census is obligatory under the British North America Act. The number of representatives which each province is entitled to have in this house, and the subsidy which the federal government pays to the western provinces, are based on the information obtained at this census. While this of course does not present insuperable difficulties, the amendment of the constitution at any time is a matter that should be most carefully considered.
Postponement of the census would require an amendment of the British North America Act not only by both houses of this parliament but also by the British parliament.
It is interesting to note that one of the first acts of the United States in relation to their defence preparations was to declare the census bureau a war department so that it could not be interfered with. All census employees there are exempt from any military service unless or until released from census duties. However we propose to overcome this by the selection of personnel.
The majority of the communications which I have received or the newspaper editorials and articles which have been published opposing the census this year, have been based largely on one or other of the arguments, that it is simply a matter of head counting or that the expense can be saved. I have already dealt with this first objection and 
shown that the intended census is far from a mere tabulation of our population. It is a much needed statistical basis for a full consideration of all economic and social problems.
The idea of saving money by postponement of the census is attractive, but it is not well founded. If the money which would be spent would in any degree lessen the effectiveness of our war effort, you can be assured that neither I nor any one of my colleagues would contemplate proceeding with the census for one moment, and of course the same is true of every member of this house. We definitely believe, however, that the value of the census to the economic life of this country far outweighs the immediate saving "of the money which would be spent on a census this year. I say immediate saving because this money will have to be spent, if not this year, then next year or the year after or at a still more distant time. If long delayed the census would lose much of its real value. I might add that already approximately $100,000 have been spent in preparatory work for the census. The total cost will be spread over approximately four years although the greatest expenditure of course will take place this coming year.
The large number of enumerators who will be required will be taken entirely from among those people who would not be available or suited for war work. We propose to use ex-service men and capable women where practicable.' There will be no necessity for any men to be drafted or withheld from industry because of the census. The enumerators will be selected on broad, general principles, from people of all classes who are able and available, and partisanship in this selection will be avoided. Instructions to the census commissioners will be definite in these respects.
We have had suggestions from different quarters that the census might be taken by workers on a voluntary basis. We appreciate to the full the spirit which has prompted these offers. The nature of the census, however, requires a regimentation of staff which would be very difficult if the workers were on a voluntary basis. It is necessary that the commissioners be in a position to direct their enumerators to do certain things at certain times, and, with all respect to a voluntary organization, I think' the house will agree with me that many difficulties would result if voluntary workers were employed. One group which made an offer of assistance for little or no fee was the Canadian Teachers' Federation. There is perhaps no group in this country who are better able to carry out the census work or complete the intricate forms

necessary, but the census must be taken in June and it will take several weeks to instruct the enumerators before that time.
Secrecy is an essential part of the census. Oaths of secrecy must be taken by all enumerators and, for this as well as other reasons, it is essential that the commissioners be able to select enumerators having regard to their suitability. This might be extremely difficult if the work were handled through a voluntary organization.
In considering the problems to which the war is giving rise, it is most desirable that complete up-to-date information as to our economic situation be available not only for ourselves but for our allies. One illustration of this is the desirability of having complete knowledge of the situation in regard to western agriculture at the earliest possible moment so that we may deal with agricultural problems, such as wheat, with all available facts before us.
Full consideration has been given to the fact that many of our enlisted men are away from home. Arrangements have been made that all abroad as well as in Canada will be enumerated, and the information included for their ordinary place of residence.
The reasons for the census this year may be briefly stated as follows:
Failure to take the census would impair the working of the principle of representation by population. It is, therefore, a constitutional necessity.
It is a financial necessity for the purpose of determining provincial subsidies.
It is a practical necessity because of the need of comprehensive factual information on innumerable subjects by provincial governments as well as the federal.
The census is the basis of all our statistics dealing with the problems of population.
With our large immigrant population a census is the only means of determining the rate of assimilation and is therefore essential for determining immigration policy. This, incidentally, may be very much to the front after the war.
The information obtained as to occupation, employment and earnings of our citizens is essential to competent administration of social welfare legislation. This information will be particularly necessary in regard to the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The census is essential to educational administration in the provinces because the information obtained is required for the determination of present and future school problems.
The decennial census is the factual basis of the agricultural policy of the ten departments of agriculture of this country. Annual sample investigations have been made but
these are unsatisfactory unless a comparison is possible with complete statistics for a decennial period.
The census of trading and service establishments has been found most valuable in the legislative work of parliament in recent years and it cannot be given up without serious loss to the country.
The usefulness of the census extends over a ten-year period. It affords much needed information to foreign countries as well as to our own people concerning developments and opportunities of investment, trade and the like.
Unless the decennial census is taken there will be many special statistical investigations required and these in all would be very much more expensive than a single census.
The census has become an integral part of our government operations. It is just as important as hundreds of functions of other departments which are being carried on from day to day unquestioned. The fact that the census occurs only once in ten years should not obscure this fact, and opposition to the taking of the census should not be based on this premise without complete evaluation of the essential factors which require a census.
The government has decided that for these and other reasons the decennial census should be taken this year. Arrangements are being made accordingly.

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, March 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for committee of supply.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is just three weeks ago to-day since this motion was before the house on a former occasion. At six o'clock that afternoon I was attempting to discuss the plight of the agricultural industry throughout Canada. I had stated among other things that the revenue of the average farm was insufficient to meet overhead expenses and maintain a reasonable standard of living for the farmer and his family. In proof of that statement I referred to figures in the Sirois report which showed clearly that for many years the share of the national income which the farmer has been obtaining ranged from eight to eleven per cent. A supplementary report to the Sirois report, recently brought down, shows that for the years 1936 to 1940 the farmers' share of the national income had not increased but had, in fact, been a little less than in 1936, the final year of the former period.
I had also stated at that time that because of certain action on the part of the administration, and on the other hand because of certain lack of action by the administration, there was a feeling of resentment in the mind of the farming community of Canada against the present government. As an indication of that I instanced a meeting held in the city of London at which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) attended and spoke. The minister said at that time that I had left for home too soon. I am afraid that practically everyone who attended that meeting went home too soon to get any satisfaction either from the minister or from those who were present. I am afraid the minister has not properly gauged public opinion throughout Ontario, for this meeting was representative of the farmers of western Ontario. Those farmers went there that day with open minds, I believe; they hoped and expected that the minister would lay down some policy which would be of benefit to the agricultural industry in that section, and, in fact, in all Canada; but I know from those to whom I have talked that they were not satisfied; in fact, I have heard of no one yet who went away at all satisfied.
As proof of this I point out that shortly afterwards organized agriculture came to Ottawa to present their views and to ask certain things from the Prime Minister himself. The Minister of Agriculture will remember, as a great many in this house do who
attended that meeting, that the minister of agriculture of Ontario voiced dissatisfaction with the statements which were made at that time, and the Ontario government have gone further and taken certain steps by way of bonusing cheese and bacon to help overcome the difficulties under which agriculture in Ontario has been labouring. That action was endorsed by all parties in the Ontario legislature, although they have stated both in the legislature and on the public platform that they thought this action should have been taken by the federal rather than by the provincial authority.
That the government feared that conditions arising out of the present struggle would add to the fanners' difficulties was made apparent at the beginning of the war, by its action in setting up different boards to deal with farm problems, and more particularly the problem of marketing farm products. A number of boards were set up; the first, I believe, was that known as the agricultural supplies board. From that board there emerged a number of supplementary boards to deal with farmers' problems and the problems of marketing farm products. The bacon board was set up, and shortly afterwards the dairy products board, a fruit and vegetable board, a seed supply committee and a fertilizer committee among others. I point out, as I believe has been done before, that the personnel of these boards ranges in number from three to eight each, yet there has not been a single producer or representative of any farm producer organization placed on any of these boards from that time to this. That criticism should be levelled particularly against the action of the government in setting up the bacon board and the dairy products board, because these two boards have wide powers, and they deal particularly with the marketing of farm products. The bacon board, for example, was given wide powers in the control of exports, and was also vested with the authority and the duty of regulating hog prices, having regard to the price which was received for bacon.
Up to the beginning of the war, exports of bacon were carried on through the ordinary channels of trade, but shortly after the war began, an agreement was entered into between the government of Canada and the British supplies board relating to the export of bacon to the United Kingdom at a set price of $18.01 per hundredweight at the seaboard. The first bulletin which came out led the farmers to believe that they would receive a set price for the hogs which they produced and marketed during that year. Unfortunately, however, that was not realized. There were continual fluctuations during that year, and
Supply-State of Agriculture

the farmers as a result were very much disappointed. They made their plans on the basis of a set price, and have been unable to realize since then a price which netted them a reasonable profit.
Last fall the Minister of Agriculture went to Great Britain where he entered into a new agreement with the British supplies board or the British government whereby prices on bacon shipped from Canada to the United Kingdom were reduced by the sum of $2.19 per hundredweight. That has resulted, as everyone knows, in a reduction in hog prices to the farmer. It has been hard medicine for the farmers to take. No one will suggest for a moment, farmers least of all, that Britain itself should be required to pay higher prices. Everyone realizes that the British people are doing their utmost in an all-out effort, and that over there they are making sacrifices the like of which we in this country know nothing about. It is, however, still true that the farmers of Canada have been asked to produce some 425 million pounds of bacon to be shipped to Great Britain at prices which will not repay them the cost of production, and which, indeed, mean a loss. Everyone will admit that foodstuffs are just as great a necessity for our war effort as any other line of production. But the farmers are not receiving the same treatment as other producers in this country, and that is what troubles them and the thing to which they object. I stated the other day, and I repeat, that munitions of all kinds are being purchased from the producer at prices which cover the cost of production plus a reasonable profit. Labour is also receiving prices which it realized during the years 1926 to 1929, giving to labour an entirely different basis from that which the farmer is enjoying.
I want to speak for a moment about the activities of the dairy products board. This is another board which was set up without any representation of producers or of any dairy organization in Canada. They were given authority and power to control exports of dairy products, and particularly exports of cheese. They have set up a number of regulations, which I shall not discuss at this time-regulations which I am afraid are taking the exporting of cheese out of the hands of the ordinary exporter and placing it very largely in the hands of two or three big exporting firms.
I Should like to ask a further question of the administration, a question which is being asked by farmers throughout the dominion. Were butter prices pegged on the recommendation of the dairy products board, or were they pegged because of the statistics given to the war-time prices and trade board 
by the dairy products board? What prompted the idea? I should like to know, as well, why the same basis was not employed in determining the pegged price of butter as has been employed in pegging the price of labour.
Between the years 1926 and 1929, which served as a basis for the pegging of labour prices, the average high for butter stood at 44-6 cents and the average low at 38 cents, making an average, between high and low in those years, of a price about five cents higher than the pegged price of butter to-day. The minister made a statement at London, and I believe he has since repeated it in the house, that butter prices were pegged largely to control speculation, and to ensure that speculators did not make unreasonable profits. I have no brief whatever for speculators, but I believe in times past they have performed a useful function by entering the market and taking off surpluses -which would have depressed butter prices to a point much lower than they went last summer, or than they have been in years past.
I believe it would have been a more reasonable idea-and perhaps this was in the minds of the dairy products board when the price of butter was pegged-to make some effort to prevent undue increases in the production of butter, and a corresponding reduction in the production of cheese. Since that time the government has seen fit to add additional powers to those already enjoyed by the dairy products board. I refer to the power to set minimum prices for butter. It seems to me that this is an important prerogative to give to any board, particularly when it has among its number no representative from the producers.
I should like to know whether, when the price of butter was pegged a short time ago, the war-time prices and trade board consulted the national dairy council. I should like to know whether it consulted any of the dairy associations throughout Canada, or whether it took it upon itself to make the price at the suggestion of the minister. If it was not done in that way, then how was it done? When they do set a minimum price, as they no doubt intend to do, I should like to know on what basis such action would be taken.
Will they, as I suggest they should, meet any of the dairy organizations in Canada? Will they take into their counsel representatives of the national dairy council, the eastern dairymen's association, the western dairymen's association or other like associations I could name? I suggest to the government here and now that before minimum prices are set by the board, its personnel should be increased, and that a representative of some of the producer organizations should be placed upon

Supply-Stale of Agriculture
the board, so that producers might have at least some reasonable hope that they would receive a fair deal.
I would say a further word about the agricultural supplies board, the main body.
I believe that board is, to a great extent, composed of men in the Department of Agriculture. They are men for whom I have a high regard, men who are well posted in agricultural matters. I believe, however, they have failed in one aspect more than in any other. The farmers themselves are unable to forecast the demands and needs of any particular market. This is particularly true in war-time. The average farmer on the back concessions has no way of knowing what demand there will be for the production of butter or cheese or bacon or any other farm product. The only people who can form a just estimate of the needs of the market are in the Department of Agriculture itself. I believe the government and this board have failed in not guiding the farmers in the type of production which should be carried on, particularly having regard to the needs of British and Canadian markets.
For many years past-in fact, ever since I can remember-the prevailing idea in the marketing of farm products has been that that marketing must be governed by the law of supply and demand. I am afraid to-day that is an inefficient method of fixing a price structure for agricultural products. It simply means that in all lines of farm production we have cycles of plenty and cycles of shortage. Unfortunately the farmer loses at both ends. When there is plenty, or when there is a surplus on the market, prices fall below the price of production. When there is a shortage, unfortunately the farmer usually has little to sell, because that is the very condition which creates the shortage.
Agriculture is the only industry in Canada I know of which does not enjoy some sort of price-maintenance scheme. Labour unions have their union scale of wages; they have their eight-hour day, and their hours of labour regulations. The price paid for manufactured goods bears some relationship to the cost of production plus profit. Civil servants and salaried people know at the beginning of the year what their incomes will be during that year. Retailers, wholesalers and others in distribution businesses make mark-ups from time to time. Doctors, lawyers and other professional men have schedules of fees to which they adhere more or less closely. Rates for all types of public services-freight rates, passenger rates, telephone rates, water rates, gas rates-are set by government bodies, such as the board of transport commissioners. The farmer is the only one who is at a disadvantage
because he still employs an outmoded and antiquated method of setting the price structure which from time to time he enjoys.
There are one or two further factors which enter into the determination of the price structure of farm products. One of those factors is this: The price received for the exportable surplus to a very great extent determines the domestic price of farm products. I have in my hand a circular sent out by the bureau of statistics showing the percentages of farm products which from time to time have been exported. For the information of the house I shall place on record the figures for 1939, the last year for which information is available:

Yet it was the 11 per cent of live stock and animal products exported which set the domestic prices paid for those products throughout Canada. It seems to me that this is clearly a case of the tail wagging the dog. Until some other method is devised to determine the farm price structure, the farmer will never enjoy the prosperity to which he is entitled.
Another factor which affects the farm price structure is the competition of imported goods of different kinds in the home market. This is particularly apparent in the case of fruits and vegetables. I shall not, however, deal with this matter in detail because it will be referred to later on.
I should like to mention one other matter which I think is important, namely, the importation of vegetable oils. For the past few years we have been importing immense quantities of vegetable oils which come into direct competition with animal fats produced in Canada. You cannot turn on the radio during the day without hearing these imported oil products such as crisco and so on, being advertised. On more than one occasion I have suggested to the present administration that a similar advertising campaign should be carried on for animal fats such as lard. The United States has undertaken such a campaign and has put out a circular, a copy of which I have in my office, advocating the use of lard instead of oleomargarine and vegetable oils of different kinds. To-day lard is selling in carload lots for as low as four and a half cents a pound when it is being bought in the carcas from the farmer at nine to nine and a half cents a pound. Whatever the price may be, the price of the whole hog is lowered because the packer must take a loss
Supply-State of Agriculture

on the lard produced from the particular animal. If I had the time I could quote the prices paid for tallow, grease and so on, but I will leave this for other hon. members who will follow.
One of the greatest difficulties faced by the farmer in connection with his price structure is the rapid and violent fluctuations which take place from time to time. Throughout the years there has been a constantly widening margin between producer and consumer prices. I do not know who can be blamed for that, but it is undoubtedly true. The farmer must plan for some time ahead if he is to produce wheat, dairy products, beef, pork, fruits, vegetables or any other product. If prices change in the meantime, he finds that when his product goes on the market he must accept a price which is much lower than he expected and at which he cannot make a profit. I believe, if farm prices could be stabilized-and I am not asking that they be stabilized at excessive figures-the farmer would be in a much better position and could make his plans ahead with confidence.
The other day the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) outlined the wheat policy of this government. I realize that this is an important matter, but I do not intend to deal with it at any length. The hon. member who will second the amendment which I propose to move in a few minutes, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), is, I believe, one of the best authorities on wheat problems in this house. From time to time the suggestions which he has made have been accepted by this and former governments. I am going to leave it to him to deal with this question of wheat.
There is, however, one thing I wish to say, and I shall try to condense it into one or two sentences. I believe the farmers of eastern Canada will resent most bitterly the proposal of the government to pay the western producers of coarse grains a bonus of $2 an acre when those grains will be fed to live stock which will compete with stock from eastern Canada where no bonus is being paid. How my Liberal friends from rural ridings in eastern Canada will be able to sit quietly by without making any protest is beyond my imagination. I have talked to several of them, and I know they appreciate the disadvantages under which the eastern producers of grain will be placed by this move on the part of the government. Already the western hog producer is feeding grain which he cannot sell at prices sufficient to pay him his cost of production. If he is to be bonused, [Mr. Senn.1
I am afraid it will result in the total demoralization and ultimate ruin of agriculture throughout the Dominion of Canada.
I do not believe that this particular programme is popular in all parts of the west. If I am correctly informed, delegations have arrived in Ottawa since the programme was announced to protest against it. I have here a report which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post of March 20, headed, "Motion against wheat programme at Abernethy." I believe Abernethy is either in the constituency of the Minister of Agriculture or very close to it.

speechtext: It is my second closest home town.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Here is the report:
A resolution protesting against the recently announced federal wheat marketing policy was passed at a public meeting held under the auspices of the local wheat pool committee here Saturday.
With Elton Dick presiding, discussion was lengthy, those present, comprising some thirty farmers of the district who struggled through the worst blizzard of the season to attend, opposing the dominion government programme and expressing approval of the policy endorsed by the Saskatchewan legislature.
After considering a number of resolutions, the following was finally adopted as the consensus of opinion of the gathering:
"Be it resolved that we, the villagers and farmers of the Abernethy district, recommend that the worm turn now on the prairie, as it did about two months ago in London, Toronto and Ottawa, all in old Ontario, by requesting the Saskatchewan cooperative conference recommend to president Hannam that an emergency assemblage of all the agricultural confederated clans of Canada be called forthwith to march on Ottawa and present our views, not only on this latest evidence on how much our present federal government really does love the wheat growers of the west, but also the still hangover problem of bacon and butter and allied questions. some of which call for immediate elucidation and possible remedial action."
I am going to leave it as it stands. I think it demonstrates most clearly that the announced wheat policy is not popular throughout the west, and it certainly is unpopular here.
Another difficulty which faces Canadian agriculture is the shortage of farm labour. Farmers have never been able to compete with industry in the labour market. The hours of labour on the farm must of necessity be longer than in the factory. With the present levels of farm prices the farmer cannot possibly pay wages equal to those enjoyed by workers in the city. This condition is aggravated by the necessities of war. Referring again to the Sirois report, and taking the year 1940 as a basis, I find that the estimated cash expenditure of the average farm is $453 for the year. Included in those cash expendi-

Supply

State oj Agriculture
tures are wages, municipal taxes, threshing bills, blacksmith bills, bills for repairs and a number of other items. It will be seen that the farmer cannot pay much for labour.
All during the past year there has been a constant exodus of farm labour and sons of farmers to the cities where employment can be obtained at wages far above anything the farmer can pay. Only the day before yesterday I heard a radio broadcast comment upon the large number of farm sales being advertised in our weekly press. This is an indication of what is taking place on the farms of Ontario where owners are finding it impossible to carry on because of a lack of farm help. In my opinion such a condition of affairs must ultimately result in a shortage of production on the farms and in a lack of proper cultivation. After all, it is the production and marketing of primary products which to a very large extent determines the buying power of any nation. Of the four great primary industries in Canada, agriculture, mining, fishing and lumbering, agriculture is the only one which produces without depleting our resources. Each year vast quantities of agricultural products are produced from the soil; and if proper methods of fertilization, crop rotation and cultivation are practised, the soil will not be depleted. Considerable cost is incurred in seeding, harvesting, processing and marketing our farm products, and unless and until they can be marketed at prices which will pay the cost of production and provide a reasonable profit, neither agriculture nor any other industry in the country can obtain its maximum prosperity nor can Canada exert its maximum war effort. Recently Mr. David Lloyd George made in the House of Commons in England a speech in which he said:
We must see that the farmer gets a reasonable return. It is no use thinking you can compel him to cultivate his ground to the utmost; you must make it worth his while. You must bring him along as a willing helper.
There are four arms of war services-the army, the navy and the air force, and _ the fourth is equally important, namely, agriculture. Foodstuffs are necessary. The very life and security of the empire depends upon it. If it fails, the other three cannot succeed. '
There is no more loyal person in Canada than the farmer. His surroundings and environment promote love of country and lead him to cherish the soil from which he sprang and from which he wrests his living by the sweat of his brow. No people are more anxious to do their full share in our war effort, and our farmers feel most keenly their inability to subscribe to war charities and to purchase government securities at this critical time. I cannot urge upon the government too strongly the imperative duty
that confronts our government to take measures to provide conditions in agriculture which will enable this important element in our national life to do their share in the great effort in which we are engaged.
I therefore beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley):
That all the words after "that" in the motion be struck out, and that the following be substituted therefor:
it be resolved that the government should take immediate steps to create a parity of prices as between agricultural and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture and in order that it may receive a just and fair return, and thus be enabled to make that contribution to Canada's war effort which is so desirable, and which our agricultural population so greatly desire to make.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to associate myself with the mover of this amendment, the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn), who, I think, has covered very well the whole field of agriculture and more particularly that branch which affects eastern Canada-the dairy industry, butter and cheese; live stock, bacon and hog prices. He also dealt with the agricultural boards that have been set up by the government, and showed the results of their actions.
I think it is apparent to all of us, after
listening to the hon. member and after what we have heard in the house and seen in the press in the last few days, that the plight of agriculture is a problem second in importance only to that of the war. I could substantiate that by quoting from the western press and showing what happened in the legislature of Saskatchewan, which on a motion to adjourn to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, as it was designated, took a whole day to discuss the problem of agriculture. I could cite other quotations from newspapers all over the country to show that the whole of Canada is agitated over this problem and realizes that it is second in importance only to that of the war.
Practically 60 per cent of the population of Canada depends upon agriculture, and 75 per cent of the farmers of western Canada are directly dependent upon wheat. During the last ten years the farmers of western Canada have had some difficulty in carrying on; but let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of the west are just as anxious and willing as any other class of people in Canada to-day to sacrifice and do their part in winning this war. In support of that statement I want to put on record a report from the director of public information which came to hand last Friday. Under the heading of "Gifts from far and near to
Supply-State of Agriculture

Canada's cause," it says that three contributions of SI,000 each have been received, and it names as one of these contributors Mr. E. C. Skinner of Indian Head, a pioneer farmer of that district and a resident of my constituency. I am pleased indeed to put that on record. He is a farmer who is anxious and willing to do his part in this war.
If we had time to review agriculture over a number of years, say the last thirty-five years, we would find that there have been periods of prosperity among agriculturists in Canada, but I regret to say that we would also find that there have been times of depression, and these depression periods have taken a heavy toll. If we look at the situation to-day, we may well become alarmed, for the problem of agriculture to-day is so acute that it is now a direct responsibility of this government-and they are not doing very much to adjust and square it away. Whatever policy is adopted by the government must be of a permanent nature, based on a long-range view.
In the period from 1930 to 1935 the Bennett government, when agriculture was in similar circumstances to those prevailing to-day, tried to do much for the farmer. It will be recalled that the Bennett government introduced many measures for the benefit of the farmers which were not supported by the Liberals who then were sitting on this side of the house. Since 1935. when there was a change of government, conditions have gradually grown worse until to-day we have a situation where the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat is only 50 per cent of what it was in 1926.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The worst condition in which agriculture has found itself, and I trust that the hon. member who is interrupting will stay glued to his seat until I get through, because he will have his chance to speak later on.
Since 1939, less than two years ago, we find from the index price of materials that there has been an increase of 8 per cent on the average in the prices of commodities the farmer has to buy. I will mention a few items. The cost of machinery and equipment has increased 26 points over 1939; the cost of transportation has increased several points; building materials have gone up 29 points. Clothing, hosiery and women's 
apparel have gone up 16 points, and drugs 35 points. I could quote many similar increases if I had the time.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat referred to the increase in wages paid to labour, and the index shows that, compared with 1926, there is an advance of 91 per cent. The farmer sees no reason why an approximate balance should not be maintained between the wages obtained by factory workers and the prices he receives for his goods. If that principle were applied, on the basis of the increases received by labour, a bushel of wheat should now be worth $1.39 instead of 70 cents at Fort William; bacon should be $10.50 per 100 pounds, instead of $8.30; butter should be 49 cents a pound instead of about 37 cents. Apparently the government has lagged during all the last two or three years, instead of bringing into operation some method of reducing this disparity. Prices of the commodities the farmer has to buy have advanced, and prices of the commodities he sells have been declining. A parity of prices should be reached. I am sure that the farmers of western Canada would not care if wheat went down to 25 cents a bushel so long as the prices of the commodities which they have to buy, and which go into their costs of production, went down to an equivalent extent.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) knows the situation. The agriculturists of Canada, and particularly the people of the west, are looking to him more than to any other member of the government to correct the present state of affairs. Why does he not take the action which he knows is necessary and which he has the power to take?
I appeal to his supporters to put pressure on him in that regard. I recall, as the house will recall, some of the statements and promises he has made in this chamber and when speaking in western Canada. We remember a speech which he made in this house warning the implement companies of what would happen if they did not reduce prices of implements. What happened? We have to-day a condition whereby it takes 650 bushels of wheat to buy a binder.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame 1

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister knows that grain prices should be higher. I can here quote from a newspaper of January 30, in which it is stated that the Minister of Agriculture said that prices should be higher all along the line: he spoke to that effect when a delegation representative of the Canadian federation of agriculture met the entire cabinet

Supply-State of Agriculture
in Ottawa. I have other quotations here to show that he knows that prices should be higher all along the line.
The hon. member who spoke before me dealt, as I have said, with that branch of agriculture which is more or less diversified and is of particular interest to the east. I come now to this question of wheat. What about it?
This afternoon I am going to offer the house something new. I do not hesitate to do so, because on many occasions I have made original suggestions which, although described by some hon. members opposite as moonshine, have been put on the statute books, even by the present government, and within the last two years.
Before presenting the suggestion, however, I wish briefly to review the situation since 1939. I recall the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) in which he outlined the situation with respect to wheat. Let me say this, that no matter what we adopt as a national policy, every branch of agriculture must be considered and the whole problem dealt with from the long-range point of view. I would encourage the cooperation of every branch of agriculture.
But I wish first to protest against what has been going on in this city and outside this house during the last two or three weeks. The other day, when I asked that the house should have an opportunity on a certain day of discussing this all-important question of wheat, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) replied that the ministers were too busy, and that they had had to be in their seats while the discussion was going on upon the resolution preceding the bill which is before us to-day. Well, we know the more important ministers have not been in their seats. I refer particularly to the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We know they have been meeting groups from western Canada. They have conferred with western Liberals, representatives of the western governments, representatives of municipal organizations, and others. We know that what I would call a hole-and-corner business has been going on. That is evident from the reports in the press. To show the house what a dictatorship this is, may I quote from the Ottawa Journal, which, in its issue of March 26, has this to say:
Start Wheat Policy.
Regina, March 25.-Machinery for preliminary operation of the federal wheat policy aimed at reducing acreage seeded to wheat this year was set in motion to-day immediately upon return of J. J. McGurran, secretary of the Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities, from Ottawa.
Why is this announcement made out there? The machinery is all set up, and we as a parliament have to swallow it, to agree to it when the minister has already started it in the west. The announcement could have been made here long ago. This problem did not arise overnight; it has been with us for months, and the announcement should have been made in this house; for we, as members representing western constituencies, know the situation as well as many of these men who have been in these hole-and-corner meetings.
The situation caused by the accumulation of wheat, this surplus of which we hear so much, is pretty well known, and it is not necessary for me to comment on it. I would, however, say this, that at the present time the farmer is not in a position immediately to adjust his system of operation to the extent of 35 per cent reduction in the seeded acreage. I contend that this is too drastic a step to ask them to take in one year. If the process had been spread over a number of years, it might have been effective and the farmers would the more readily have fallen into line.
Since last fall many and various suggestions have been made to the government by various organizations-provincial governments, municipalities, pools, and others. I am in accord with quite a number of the suggestions and recommendations which have been made, for the simple reason that I, two or three years ago, proposed most of them. I am in accord, first of all, with the quota system or permit system as recommended by the western pools and the provincial governments. Why? I have here a statement taken from Hansard, 1934, pages 375-6, which reports the suggestion I then made of a permit system in order to curtail the production of wheat. I said at that time that my plan was (a) to determine the requirements by adding to the export quota the domestic requirements, and (b) to determine the acreage seed required to produce wheat in one year; and, dividing (a) by (b), to arrive at the number of bushels to be delivered under the permit. We were in difficulties in 1935. as hon. members will remember; and when I tried to sell the idea to my leader, he thought that it might be a little drastic, and that the farmers were not prepared to submit to any enforced restriction of production. However, had that scheme been brought into force at that time, our situation to-day would have been much better.
An increase in the price to 85 cents per bushel has been suggested by the government of Saskatchewan. I certainly will support that. I have always said that the price should be around 90 cents; that 70 cents was not sufficient. Had the government set it at 85 cents and carried out the processing tax of 50
Supply-State of Agriculture

cents a bushel, they would have arrived at a price of more than 90 cents a bushel, and the result would have been much more satisfactory than what they propose to do.
It has been suggested that storage on the farm should be continued. I suggested that two years ago. Financing the farmers to build bins on their farms to earn the storage is something that should be carried to the limit, because they would have the grain where it should be stored. I shall have something to say again with respect to the processing tax. It is my baby, so to speak, and I am going to boost it on every occasion that offers.
I wish to come for a moment or two to a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture, who is smiling. I may say something that will change his smile. The other evening he outlined the policy. May I say to him, with regard to his suggestion of a system for bonusing summer-fallowing of wheat land that is not seeded, that he is suggesting something which a great many farmers, and good ones too, because there are many good farmers out there, have already undertaken on their own initiative. They have already adjusted their operations. Seeing what was happening to the market, prices of the surplus

and we know that when the surplus increases the price goes down, because that is simply a part of the law of supply and demand- many farmers have already adjusted themselves to the changed situation, and they made the adjustment long before the minister thought about it.
I might cite my own case. I am going to summer-fallow 725 acres; I have a contract in my office to have it done. Last year we sowed only 540 acres of wheat on that farm. This simply shows that many farmers have already begun to adjust themselves to conditions.
The minister speaks about farm income remaining around 8325,000,000. He provides for taking only 230,000,000 bushels this year at a net price to the farmer of 50 cents. That brings the income to $115,000,000, but he compensates by summer-fallowing to the extent of $36,000,000, and it is estimated that from coarse grain there may be another $19,000,000, making $170,000,000. This is with reference to the western farmers. He is short $155,000,000, which must be made up from some other source, but in doing this his objective is to reduce the seeded acreage by
9.000.	000 acres which, at an average of fifteen bushels, which is quite possible, would give
135.000.	000 bushels less. At 50 cents a bushel, this would be $67,000,000. He compensates $36,000,000, so that there is a difference of $31,000,000.

As a matter of fact, what the 290,000 farmers in the west are being asked to do is to live on the proceeds of 65 per cent of last year's seeded wheat acreage. That cannot be done. The minimum income on which the western farmers can live would be the revenue from the sale of wheat alone amounting to $150,000,000. They did not get by very well last year when practically all their wheat was delivered, netting them over $250,000,000. What should be done therefore, if it is desired to maintain the income of the farmers and enable them to get by, would be to take
230,000,000 bushels of wheat and make the price 85 cents, as the province of Saskatchewan and the pools have asked. A price of 85 cents would net a little more than $150,000,000.
I am not worrying very much about surplus wheat. It may be a blessing in disguise, because we know that wars have not been lost in consequence of having a great surplus of wheat or of other foodstuffs. The danger lies the other way. A little later, perhaps to-morrow, we may have occasion to review the minister's proposal in greater detail-that is, the bonusing of a part of the wheat acreage of last year for summer-fallowing. I would, however, say this in passing. The minister certainly discriminates against the small farmer, the man with a half section. The farmer with 300 acres under cultivation last year cropped 120 acres; he had coarse grains to the extent of 60 acres and he summer-fallowed 120 acres. This year he will crop 80 acres; coarse grain will account for 60 acres; and he will summer-fallow 160 acres. Taking an average of 10 bushels to the acre- and I am being kind to the minister because they will get more than that-he will have 40 acres less, which at 10 bushels to the acre would mean 400 bushels, and at 50 cents a bushel this would represent $200 to the small farmer. It would cost him at least $2 an acre to summer-fallow the 40 acres, which would be $80. He has to do most of it by horsepower. His compensation, 40 acres at 84 an acre, amounts to $160, so that his net return is less by $120. If I had time to review the figures for the farmer with 1,000 acres,
I could show that on a similar basis, reducing his return by 30 per cent, he is only out $240 when he gets his compensation. That is, taking 1,000 acres as against 300 acres, he is only out double, which is not proportionate.
The minister for many years has been getting a vote on account of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. He has been given $3,000,000 in some years, the purpose being to bring a part of the province of Saskatchewan out of the dust-bowl. Now he asks the

Supply-State oj Agriculture
fanners out there to reduce their seeded acreage by 9,000,000 acres, and at one swoop he is going to bring back into the dust-bowl
9,000,000 acres more on the 1st of July. God help the people out there if winds prevail as they have been doing for some years, with 9,000,000 acres more of blackened land turned to the sun. The money he has been spending will go for naught if he pursues the policy he is following. Two years ago, in discussing the act, he said that the whole problem was to save the small farmer, and now he is discriminating against the small farmer. I understand from reports in the press that he is going to argue that this new proposal means 86 cents for wheat. I suggest that he will have quite a time persuading some of the farmers out there that this is so, because they will proceed along their own lines more or less, although they are willing to cooperate if anything reasonable is brought forward. Many will receive the bonus who are not entitled to it. The minister did not tell us, but I suppose he will give us some idea to-morrow regarding the cost of administration.
I have read a quotation showing that he will employ the municipalities. The municipalities are pretty well loaded up now with work. I do not know what he will do. That policy should have been announced here instead of in Regina. I should like to know what it will cost to have inspectors and supervisors, and he is even asking the municipalities to do that work. He is going to set up a machine such as we have never known before. We have already had experience with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. There are 290,000 farmers to be inspected and the inspectors will have a nice job.
Let me now come to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He gave a realistic picture of the situation. First, dealing with the surplus and deliveries of the last crop, he said that the quota system had been generally satisfactory. I was pleased to hear that.
The farm storage is working out satisfactorily ; he said the farmers were holding their grain to get the storage. I was pleased to hear that. He referred to the increased acreage following the last war. That increase came about from a patriotic point of view; an appeal was made to the farmers to increase their seeded acreage of wheat as a contribution to the war effort. He referred to the possible disappearance next year of 307 million bushels, dealing with it from the point of view of domestic seed and feed and possible export. Then he dealt
with the carryover of 550 million bushels. The	total	storage he	figured	out	at around582	million bushels.	Then	he	made thestatement	that the government's	investmentwas	now	$400,000,000	which	required between $50,000,000 and $60,000,000-nearer $60,000,000-a year to carry it.
He stated that they are going to take only 230 million in order to encourage a reduction in the seeded acreage. The 70-cent price remains; it is not enough. The storage on the farm is paid only on the balance of the 230 million which they propose to take that is not delivered. I regret this. I think the farmer should be paid storage on all he has on his farm.
There is no change in the processing tax. I regret that. That processing tax should have been increased to 50 cents, as western provincial governments wanted. Why? Because the price of the loaf of bread should not be increased at all by reason of a 50-cent processing tax, making wheat come to $1.20 or $1.25 a bushel. The price of a loaf of bread should not be more than seven cents. There is the greatest racket going on that one can imagine in the big mill-controlled bakeries throughout Canada. There should be an investigation of them by this government. Yesterday I talked with the Canada Bread Company in this city; they make forty-six loaves of bread out of a bushel of wheat. At ten cents a loaf this comes to $4.60, whereas the farmer gets fifty cents. There is something wrong. I have talked with the mills, and they have admitted to me that the price of bread was away out of line with the price of wheat. If the processing tax were fifty cents, the price of bread should not go up at all, so we should have it because it means that at least $25,000,000 would be added to the price of the 230 million bushels. There should be an investigation into this bread business.
There are two methods by which to control production; first, by the power of the government; second, by voluntary action on the part of the producer. I believe the producers themselves will adjust their operations to meet the market and price conditions; there is no need for this action on the part of the government. Never has a question of such importance had so little discussion in this house as this all-important question of the production and marketing of grain. I refer to the pool statement when the announcement was made, that they were surprised and dismayed in the west, and they go on and state why.
In the few minutes remaining at my disposal I wish to offer something constructive.
Supply-State oj Agriculture

I am going to offer now what I think is the first step in the solution of this problem, and I should like the house to listen.
The problem divides itself into two branches: first, production, and second, marketing. By the first the farmer cultivates his fields, seeds and harvests the grain, and delivers it to the elevator. By the second the elevator takes in the grain, weighs, stores, ships and sells it. The farmer works at less than cost of production; and under the second, huge profits accrue to those all along the way. There are many injustices being practised. Under the present system there has prevailed a desire on the part of the elevator companies to hold the grain back in the country in order to gain the storage payment. We now have an order in council, P.C. 1225, passed on February 29 I believe, authorizing the building of 50 million bushels additional storage capacity ' at Fort William. Elevator men say it will cost about $5,000,000 to build. At prevailing rates of storage, about $4,000,000 a year will accrue to those who are building them and the capital is written off in two years. That is an outrage, and should not be permitted. I have always claimed that storage rates on grain are too high. I have here a statement made by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) last year, which goes into that fully. This storage space should be built on the farms; the farmer should be encouraged to add to his storage the 50 million bushels. That would earn him, if storage rates are what they should be, one cent a bushel a month on the farm, or $120 a year for one thousand bushels. Then this $6,000,000 would be earned by the farmers instead of by the interests at Fort William. I make this statement, that under present storage charges the whole elevator system in that western country will be paid for in less than five years.
Here is my proposal. We have a war on. The other day we had two ministers of this government opening the war services campaign in front of the national war memorial, urging women and children to save their nickels for the war. Yet here we have the government permitting a system under which certain interests are getting huge profits beyond all reason. I suggest that this government proceed to take over, commandeer if you like, all the elevators and storage space in western Canada from Fort William to the coast. They should operate it by a board;
I could name forty men in western Canada who could1 do it. Let the prevailing storage rates be paid, paying the capital out in five years. If I had time I could give figures showing how it would pay for itself at present storage rates in three and a half years, as well as pay for the operation of the scheme. This 
proposal comes to me from a late president of the grain exchange-I am permitted to use his name if I desire-and many others who are interested in the grain business. They see what has happened; they know the solution. This is nothing new; it came to me not only this year, but in 1935 when we tried to persuade Mr. Bennett to do the same thing.
What is going on? Under the annexes that are being built in western Canada we have a system under which a 30,000 bushel capacity annex is permitted to earn $2,400 a year. It costs to build not more than $2,000; it pays 120 per cent on the initial cost. Then we have the statement I have just referred to as to fifty million bushels capacity to be built in Fort William, costing not more than $5,000,000, with an earning capacity of $4,000,000 a year. That is an outrage.
I have here a statement that I should like to be permitted to read or place on Hansard because I think it is valuable information. What does this all mean? I said we should take over the whole system. These are the figures issued by the bureau of statistics recently and in the "Canada Year Book". We have 5,678 elevators in western Canada west of Fort William with a capacity of
191.000.	000 bushels, and ait an estimated value of $62,000,000. We have thirty-four terminals in Fort William and in the west-twenty-nine at Fort William and Port Arthur, four at the coast and one at Churchill. Those elevators have a capacity of 127,500,000 bushels, and are valued at $42,000,000. We have 3,000 annexes built, with an estimated space of around 80,000,000 bushels, and at a cost of $5,000,000. We now have provision for a further 50,000,000 bushels at Fort William at a cost of not more than $5,000,000.
In this computation I am not including the mills or eastern terminals at Halifax, Saint John or along the St. Lawrence river. We find that we now have in western Canada a total elevator capacity of 411,500,000 bushels, plus 50,000,000 bushels at Fort William, making a total of around 460,000,000 bushels in western Canada, at a capitalization of $120,000,000.
I have here a statement of earnings. If taken over, that system will earn $40,000,000 a year.
I have it all figured out-8,678 country elevators and annexes with a space of 266,000,000 bushels, at a rate of eight cents, making a total earning of $21,280,000. Then, there are thirty-four terminal elevators with a capacity of 127,500,000 bushels, earning $7,650,000; there are interior terminals with a space for
18.000.	000 bushels, at eight cents, making a figure earned of $1,460,000; and then there is

Supply-State of Agriculture
the 50,000,000 bushels added at Fort William, at eight cents, making $4,000,000, or a total earning of $40,000,000.
That is, in five years the estimated earnings would be over $220,000,000. I have here allowed for $17,460,000 for operating expenses. That makes so much a unit. The whole set-up will pay for itself in three and a half years, running expenses included. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated that we have an investment of $400,000,000, and that it is costing about $60,000,000 to carry it. In the way I have indicated the whole thing can be taken over as a war measure, and would accrue to the interests of the producers. Had I the time I could show where these elevators have paid for themselves, five, six and seven times over. I can tell the minister where elevators in western Canada have paid the capital investment back in one year by storage charges, elevator fees, and profits on grain, and where money has been made on those investments. They have paid for themselves in one year. The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) knows many of them. Some of those elevators are from thirty to forty years old.
This is a war measure. If this government does not do what I have suggested, if it permits a condition to prevail where it has a capital investment of $400,000,000 and a carrying charge of $60,000,000 which, at the present rate of borrowing, is equal to a debt of $1,800,000,000, and if it does not take over as I have suggested, and place this organization in operation, it will not have done its duty.
I have a statement before me setting out how I would operate it. I would operate it by a board of seven or eight members, to which the government would name the majority and the chairman. The producers in western Canada would name the remainder. It would be subdivided into three groups, one of which would manage the country elevators; the second, the terminal elevators, and the third, the export and financial end of the business. I would commandeer the pool organization in western Canada if necessary. They have an organization already set up which would run it, and run it well. This $60,000,000 now paid to carry the wheat would accrue as an asset of the people of Canada, and to the producers in western Canada. It is theirs. They have paid for it five or six times over, and I could bring figures to prove this.
I say that any government which has a capital investment in wheat of $400,000,000, costing $60,000,000 to carry, and which has an opportunity to take this great asset that really belongs to western Canada, and does
nothing, is remiss in its duty and will go down in history as being so. I shall not say more on that point at this time, because I shall have an opportunity to speak later on, and to place on record figures to show what could be done.
The other day the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) stated that the government was organizing every industry and all man-power for war purposes. Why not organize this industry? Why not put it under control? This matter should go to a committee of the house of from thirteen to fifteen members-and not to the committee on agriculture. I suggest that the government set up a committee of thirteen and send this matter to, that committee. Let the Minister of Agriculture and others appear before that committee. Let those people from western Canada who have been sitting around here in Ottawa for two weeks have a chance to appear before that committee and give us any information they may have. In that way we would get valuable information. I would take the same position as was taken in 1935 by the Liberal party when the present Minister of National Defence then sitting right here said, "We will not allow this measure to pass if we cannot have it before a committee, and get information." When it came back from committee the members had received valuable information. They did not think for one minute that such a condition had prevailed. The committee I propose would get valuable information and could report back to the house. If we could set up that committee we, as representatives of the people of the west, who have a responsibility in this House of Commons, would do something worth while.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) in the last part of his speech reminded me of two experiences, one of which I had almost forgotten. About a year ago the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was speaking in Vancouver. A man sitting in the gallery insisted upon heckling him. Finally the Minister of Justice said to him, "My friend, I used to be a good debater; at one time I won a medal in a debate in a university. I should like to have a debate with you, but really I have not the time to have it to-night." That ended the heckling.
The other incident of which I was reminded was the first time I had had the privilege of speaking to an audience of any considerable size, when I spoke on the question which has just been discussed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. It was at Winnipeg in 1910, when the livest issue in western Canada was that
Supply-State of Agriculture

of government ownership and control of elevators. Well, I am not going to say this afternoon that as a result of delivering that speech they did get government ownership and control of elevators in Manitoba. But those who come from that province will remember that in 1910 the government of Manitoba took over the elevators in that province.
