speechtext:
They operated those elevators for a time, and they stand to-day as one of the outstanding-I was going to say business failures, but probably I should say political failures-in the history of business in Canada. So that there is nothing new in the proposal that the government should take over the elevators. There is nothing new in the suggestion that so much per bushel should be paid for storage capacity in an elevator. Governments have done it before; governments have tested the principle and have proven that it is difficult for governments to operate a system of business houses such as elevators and do it any more successfully than private individuals have been able to do it.
But I did not rise to discuss the wheat question. On three occasions I have attempted to get the agriculture estimates before this house. Hon. members on the other side of the house who have been intimating that the discussion of agricultural matters has been delayed by the government forget the fact that the only estimates that have been placed before the house, other than war estimates, are the agriculture estimates, and that these were brought down at the very beginning of the session. When I brought them into the house some weeks ago I was asked by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) to outline the government policy with regard to agricultural matters. That was about half past ten o'clock at night and for half an hour I proceeded to outline the policy of this government in relation to agriculture.
On a subsequent occasion, when an effort was made to bring these estimates back before the house, objection was raised on certain grounds. On a still later occasion an effort was made to place these estimates before the house, and three weeks ago the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) rose in his place to move a vote of want of confidence in the government by way of amendment to the motion that the Speaker do now leave the

chair. My hon. friends on the other side of the house twit the members of this government and me as Minister of Agriculture with not having given them an earlier opportunity to discuss agricultural matters. I submit that the only reason we have not been discussing matters in relation to every branch of the Department of Agriculture is that there has been an effort on the part of the official opposition to see that the agriculture estimates did not properly get before the house up to the present time.
If any objection is taken to this remark, I need only recall the threat which was made the other night by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) when it was suggested that unless we did certain things, certain votes would not be permitted to pass this house. The question whether we were to have agriculture estimates was under discussion at the time that threat 'was made. Again I suggest that ever since the house opened the government has been persistent and insistent in its effort to get before this house a discussion of agricultural matters.
To-day we have been listening to discussion of an amendment couched in terms intended to put every hon. member of this house in a difficult position when voting upon it. The amendment reads:
That all the words after "that" in the motion be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
"it be resolved that the government should take immediate steps to create a parity of prices as between agricultural and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture and in order that it may receive a just and fair return, and thus be enabled to make that contribution to Canada's war effort which is so desirable, and which our agricultural population so greatly desire to make."
Apart altogether from the fact that this amendment, in the form and at the time it has been submitted to the house, is a vote of want of confidence in this government, it must be clear to all hon. members that every single suggestion contained in the amendment has been in effect ever since war was declared, indeed was in effect for at least four years before. The only reason they were not in effect during the whole of the fifteen years before war was declared is that for five years of that time our friends opposite were in power. But the suggestion in the motion that an attempt be made to bring about a parity of prices as between what the farmer has to sell and what he has to buy has in fact been consistently put forward ever since this government came into office, and more consistently since war was declared. There is no reason to pass a motion of this kind at this stage.

Supply-State of Agriculture

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why weren't better results obtained?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An hon. member asks why we did not get better results. I shall deal with the results in a few moments, but before doing so I should like to point out that this motion is an effort to block still further free discussion of the agricultural problems of Canada. It places every hon. member who sits on this side of the house and in the corner over there in the position of having to decide between voting want of confidence in the government and freely discussing agricultural matters as brought before the house in estimates. Thus there is an obstruction of free discussion of agricultural problems at this time.
If this motion were carried every hon. member of the house knows that as a vote of want of confidence it would require the government of this country to resign, it would require the holding of an election in Canada, it would require the reorganization of the government and the resetting up of policies, not only in connection with agriculture but in connection with every present-day war activity. I venture to say that there is not an hon. member of this house who, knowing that we are facing difficulties which may be increased within the next few weeks, even within the next few days, would wish to call upon the ministry to resign and thus bring about the disorganized condition which a resignation of the government under these circumstances would create.
In other words, the placing of a motion of this kind before the house at the present time makes impossible the free discussion of the problems which confront the agricultural population of Canada. Such a thing is unthinkable. I am prepared to discuss the whole agricultural problem if my hon. friends desire to have it done. It can be done quite simply by having this motion withdrawn and allowing the estimates of the Department of Agriculture to be placed before the house. Then we could discuss consistently and persistently every problem which is confronting the farmers of Canada, and every hon. member would be free to express his opinion, apart altogether from the attitude of this government toward the affairs of Canada and the empire.
I do not intend to place hon. members in a position to be able to say that I introduced into the discussion of a want of confidence motion the new policy of the government in relation to wheat. No doubt that would be the simplest way for me as Minister of Agriculture to have the principles of the policy which has been enunciated by the 14873-120
Minister of Trade and Commerce and by myself as Minister of Agriculture adopted by this house without any opportunity being afforded to hon. members to discuss it freely, without any opportunity being given to anyone to express himself by vote except under the hampering restraint of a want of confidence motion. I am not going to do that, Mr. Speaker. It is not my intention to discuss the wheat policy to-day. I shall choose an occasion when every member of this house will be free to discuss the wheat policy on its merits and not be hampered in any vote he may wish to cast by the fact that he has to vote on a motion of want of confidence in the government of Canada.
But there are a few other matters I should like to discuss, in view of the suggestions that have been made by the mover of the amendment. He stated this afternoon that organized agriculture came to Ottawa to see the Prime Minister and members of the government. Is the hon. member, who has been following agricultural matters in Canada very closely for many years, not aware of the fact that in every single year since the federation of agriculture was set up as the chamber of agriculture, later reorganized as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the executive committee of that organization has come to Ottawa immediately after the federation held its annual meeting and passed its resolutions? I repeat, they have called on the government every year since they have been an organization. It is true that this year for the first time they saw the whole cabinet, but it was not the first time they have asked to see the whole cabinet. They have asked to see the whole cabinet every year since they have been organized, and in each of the years since they have been organized some members of the government have met delegates from that organization. On some occasions members of the government were giving attention to other business when the delegation was here and not all the members of the government were able to meet the federation or the Canadian Chamber of Agriculture. But on each occasion since this government was formed I met them as Minister of Agriculture; on most occasions some other members of the government were with me, and we considered the point of view which the organization presented to the government.
I may say to the house, if it will please the leader of the opposition, who suggested the other night that he did not know just why I went to England last fall, that it was the federation of agriculture that first suggested I should go. They passed a resolution to that effect. Not only that, but they came to

Supply-State of Agriculture

Ottawa and presented the resolution. Not only did they suggest that I should go to England but they suggested that the chairman of the bacon board should also go to England. And the hon. member for Haldimand now tells the house that there is not a man on the bacon board who represents the opinion of the farm organizations of Canada. The federation of agriculture itself, at their annual meeting prior to the one just past, suggested that the Minister of Agriculture and the chairman of the bacon board should go to Great Britain and discuss with the British government the possibilities of having Canadian bacon disposed of in the British market. We acted on their suggestion and went to Great Britain and studied this question among many others.
There were other things which the federation suggested on that occasion, many of which have since been brought into effect in Canada. There were other suggestions made which we have not seen fit to bring into effect. For example, the suggestion was made on one occasion that we should have all agriculture in Canada organized under boards and that these boards should have power to legislate and to tax the farmers across Canada. We did not adopt that suggestion but we discussed it with them and gave them our opinion with regard to it. Again when they returned a year ago they suggested the same thing, and my reply to them, which was given to the press at that time, was to this effect, that at least so long as the war lasted any boards that might be contemplated in Canada to handle the marketing or disposal of farm products to the British government would be set up and controlled by the dominion government itself. Why? For the twofold reason that it is a sound principle to establish in any country that there shall be only one kind of authority with power to tax the people, and that that authority shall be a body elected by all the people within a given area. And there is only one authority that should be allowed to legislate in connection with matters having to do with the control of certain industries, and that body again should be the administration set up as a result of the votes either of the whole people or of the people of a province or municipality. For these reasons we said that we would retain this authority within the federal government rather than pass it over to them.
There is another reason. The British government to-day has a food ministry, a food board, a cereals board, boards controlling the shipment of food products to that country. All these matters are under government control. On a number of occasions since the war started it has been suggested to the

government of Canada that we should set up a similar authority on this side to deal, in respect to the particular product, with the corresponding British authority on the other side, in order to see to it that our foodstuffs are shipped from this country to Great Britain. That is the policy, Mr. Speaker, which we have been following, and many other proposals which were put up to us by the representatives of agriculture who came to us have been either embodied in legislation or acted upon by this government either before or since the representations were made to us.
This brings me to another remark made by the hon. member for Haldimand. He said that there was no representative of agriculture on the boards set up under the agricultural supplies board. I have here a copy of Hansard of May 23, 1940, and at page 169 I find a page and a half of the names of representatives of agriculture from every province who have been placed upon boards or advisory committees, set up after advisement with farm organizations and with the provincial governments, in order to advise the agricultural supplies committee of the Department of Agriculture in matters pertaining to agricultural policy. I shall not take the time to read the names; they will all be found in Hansard of last session. The representatives of agriculture there named are still acting on the various boards and carrying on their activities in relation to agricultural problems.
I can quite understand that someone in a particular province might be able to say that he belongs to a farm organization which is not represented on these boards. But when one realizes that there are agricultural organizations from one end of Canada to the other, in connection with every form of live stock undertaking, fruit growing, grain growing, every branch of agriculture; that there are organizations in each of the nine provinces, as well as organizations representing agriculture right across Canada, it will readily be seen how impossible it is to constitute a board in connection with any one branch of agriculture which would have on it a representative of all farm organizations in this dominion. But the men who are on are men who are representative of agriculture, in their capacities as officials of either the dominion Department of Agriculture, the provincial agricultural departments, organizations associated with agriculture, or organizations formed by agriculturists from one end of Canada to the other. As a matter of fact, at each of the different meetings which have been referred to by speakers, I have been confronted writh this same question. London was not the only place in Canada where we had a meeting; we had meetings in Saskatoon,

Supply-State of Agriculture
Regina, Calgary, and Montreal. Meetings were also organized or arranged for in the maritime provinces, but it was not possible to hold them because of the fact that the house was called in session when it was. They will, however, still take place. At each meeting I was confronted with the same question and answered it indicating that while some might disagree w7e believed we had agriculture represented.
When my hon. friend asks me whether we consulted with the farm organizations when we were appointing boards, or when the price of butter was being pegged, or when agreements were made with Great Britain, I answer that he does not know the farm organizations of Canada or he would not ask that question. They do not wait to be consulted, Mr. Speaker; they advise this government and make their views known to us. They are active organizations, on the job. The head of the dairy organization about which the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) asked a question comes to Ottawa, not once a year but a number of times every year.
When I look about this chamber I do not know of any group of men in Canada who more completely represent all the agricultural interests of this dominion than do hon. members who represent agricultural constituencies. It is all very well to say that we are going to set up an organization across Canada. I agree with setting up farm organizations. Any hon. member who has the interests of agriculture at heart and who lives in the rural area of his constituency will belong to the farm organizations of that constituency, and I take no exception to that. I believe in the farmers having organizations. In spite of some of the criticisms which are made of agriculture, and statements to the effect that farmers cannot stick together, I believe that there are no organizations in Canada which work more persistently at their jobs and keep closer contact with governments, both dominion and provincial, than do the farm organizations of the dominion. One does not have to invite them to Ottawa, or coax them to come to Ottawa.
As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) rather chided us over here because of the fact that, at this time, three or four most important farm organizations are represented by delegates now in this city, who have been here discussing questions which, he said, the members of this house had not had an opportunity to discuss, questions which, he said, as did the hon. member for Haldimand, should have been announced to the house. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle referred in this connection to a dispatch reporting the return 14873-1204
from Ottawa of J. J. McGurran, secretary-treasurer of the Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities, which association, by the way, represents more farmers than any other organization in that province. The rural municipalities of Saskatchewan cover the entire municipal area; every councillor that is elected is elected by the farmers of his division, and every secretary-treasurer is the hired official of the farmers of a municipality. That organization did have its representatives here discussing the wheat policy with us, as did organizations from Alberta and Manitoba. They have gone home, and after they had gone home they said what they had to say to their people. But I want to tell the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that the only reason he did not hear about it before was, as I mentioned a few moments ago, that we had tried on two or three occasions to get before this house with discussions on agricultural matters, that we had been threatened with this and that and the other delay if we did certain things in relation to the activities of this house, and that is the only circumstance which made it impossible for the matter to be discussed before in this house.
Because of what the hon. member placed on Hansard, a reference to my having met the members who are the real representatives of the people of Canada, and for that reason only, I wish to make this statement. I have discussed the wheat policy of this government with Liberal members of the house and with leading men in every one of the other groups in the house. Each of them will agree that I have expressed myself as being willing to meet other members of their group and to discuss with them the policy which the government was placing before the people and the methods under which they desired to have it administered. I had very helpful discussions with each one of the men with whom I raised the question. Their help in this matter has been of assistance; and I am sure that, after we have agreed to agree or disagree on the matter of policy, we shall have the assistance of hon. members in every part of this house in seeing to it that the policy is carried out in the spirit which is indicated by that great American who was with us the other day in the city of Toronto, when he said, before a committee of the house in Washington, "I did all I could to defeat the present President of the United States, but now he is my president." In that same spirit, after hon. members have said all they have to say against the policy of the government, when they have done-if you like-everything they can to defeat it, once we have decided what the policy is to be, we shall have the support of all
Supply-State of Agriculture

hon. members, in view of the conditions prevailing to-day, to have that policy put into operation as effectively as possible, for the time being.
It does not make any difference what branch of agriculture we are dealing with, whether it be wheat, or live stock, or dairy products: no great national long-term policy can be decided upon under conditions such as the world is passing through to-day. The policy which is decided upon must be one which will be put into effect for the season through which we are passing, and probably it will have to be varied even before the season is over to meet situations which develop from the fact that we are at war. I suggest again that when we have discussed the policy on its merits, under conditions enabling hon. members to express themselves freely, we shall have the unanimous support of all parties in this house in trying to do the best we can with whatever policy is evolved.
Another statement which was made was to the effect that there has been no control over farm prices, that we have not attempted to maintain farm prices in Canada which would be of assistance to our farming population. It was said that we should be able to plan for the stabilization of farm prices. All I wish to say with regard to that is to refer again to what I said at the beginning of my address, namely that this government, ever since the war started, and before, has been attempting to stabilize the prices of farm products to a point where farmers can exist under the very difficult conditions which prevail.
I only wish to emphasize what has been said by the two previous speakers when they contend that agriculture is having a very difficult time. I am not going to disagree with that. I do not think that anyone in this house will disagree with it. I think we all admit and admit quite freely that agriculture has been having a very difficult time since this war started and' that it was having a very difficult time for ten years before the war started.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is getting worse.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Someone says, "getting worse." Probably we should examine into that statement-it would not have been necessary to do so had the suggestion not been made.
I have before me the receipts from the sale of farm products from 1926 to 1940 in the different provinces. I am not going to weary the house by reading the table which gives the figures for each province, but I should like to give the returns from agriculture in the gross, in millions of dollars, in each of the years and then let the house judge whether conditions are getting worse or better.

The year 1926 is the year we are asked to go back to. In that year the returns from agriculture amounted to $952,000,000, in round figures. In the next year they amounted to $929,000,000. The year after that the amount was $1,058,000,000 and the year following that $922,000,000. The house will note that these figures compare very favourably throughout the four years. Then in 1930 conditions throughout the world took a difficult turn, and they did take a difficult turn in Canada. Here are the figures for the years from 1930 on:
Returns from
Year	agriculture
1930		 $630,000,000
1931		 442,000,000
1932		 377,000,000
1933		 390,000,000
1934		 481,000,000
1935		 509,000,000
1936		 569,000,000
1937		 640,000,000
1938		 647,000,000
1939		 702,000,000
1940		 714,000,000
I ask my hon. friends, is it correct to say that conditions are getting worse? They did get worse beginning in 1930 and going to 1933; but from 1933 up to the present, and more particularly during the last four years, they have been getting materially better so far as the returns are concerned. There are other figures here which I shall probably use when dealing with the wheat situation later, but I only want to give these figures to-day in order to indicate that it is not correct to say that conditions have been getting gradually worse. Conditions, so far as the returns are concerned, have been getting a little better from year to year, though not sufficiently better for the farmer to realize that there is any great improvement in his position.
I want to agree again with the two hon. members who spoke previously when they say that conditions in relation to agriculture in Canada at the present time are not good. But this government has not contributed towards making conditions worse from year to year since it came into office. We have contributed towards making them better and better.
Something was said by the hon. member for Haldimand about prices, and it has been repeated from one end of Canada to the other. I corrected it in his hearing in London but perhaps he went home earlier than I thought he did. Nevertheless he repeated it to-day. I had corrected it in each one of the meetings I referred to a few moments ago, and I say to my hon. friend that if he does not know it, if he will come to my office to-morrow morning I will show him correspondence from every section of the dominion where these

Supply-State oj Agriculture
meetings were held. I will show him correspondence up to the day the meeting was held and correspondence after the meeting was over, and if he does not agree with me, after he has read the correspondence, that people did change their minds slightly after these meetings, then I will take back what I am going to say to you now, Mr. Speaker.
The statement which the hon. member made and which was corrected was to the effect that there was S2.19 a hundredweight of a difference between the price which was arranged for this year with the British government for hogs and the price which was arranged for last year. He went on to say to-day, as he has repeated time after time, that that difference in the price for bacon was carried right back to the hog itself and that there was a similar reduction in the price of hogs to farmers.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have the figures here, and the average price for hogs for 1940, which was the year in which the other agreement was in effect, was $8.57 a hundred-average price at Toronto. Now, what has the average price been per month since this agreement came into effect? The average price in November was $8.31 a hundred; in December, $8.17 a hundred; in January, $8.31 a hundred; in February, $8.45 a hundred. That is just 12 cents a hundred lower for February of this year than the average throughout last year. And then the highest price that the farmers received in any month last year for hogs was received in the month of September. The price was $9.16 a hundred, on an average, throughout September; the price was $8.45 a hundred in February of this year as against $9.00 a hundred in February of last year. In other words, there is only 55 cents as between the price of February last year and the price of February this year, and only 12 cents between the price of February this year and the average price of last year.
That brings me back to what I stated in this house when I returned from Britain. I said that if the packers in Canada did what it was possible for them to do in the interests of agriculture in this country under that agreement the farmer would not be asked to take more than fifty cents a hundred less for his live hogs this year than he took on an average throughout last year. I say that prophecy made at that time has been more than borne out by the prices which farmers have received for hogs up to date. That situation prevailed with regard to hogs. May I say also that this war is no different from other wars in its effects upon farmers. Every war ever fought in
any period of history in any place was detrimental to the farming population both in the area in which it was fought and in the area from which their food supplies were to be secured. This war has been no exception to that. And the last war was no exception in the long run. Down to the present time the position of the farmer in relation to prices and other matters as associated with the first few months of this war has been at a level which compares fairly favourably with that of the first eighteen months of the last war. In so far as bacon and hogs are concerned, it is considerably better over the long period, because at the beginning of the last war, if I remember correctly-I am speaking from memory-hogs started at somewhere close to nine cents a pound, went down to close to six cents and then came back to nine cents again in the first fifteen months. But what has happened in this war?

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where did they go from nine cents?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And I will ask my hon.
friend where are they going from nine cents this time. No one can tell. There is only one thing that is going to make them go up, and that is to keep enough of this labour of which the hon. member for Haldimand spoke, in the factories of Canada producing munitions, aeroplanes, machines of war and supplying every man that can be put in the front line with the most efficient equipment that this war demands; that is the only thing that is going to put the price up. So I say that putting men in the factories, even if it does to a certain extent take them away from other industries for the time being, is not going to injure agriculture; it is not going to injure Canada, but is going to be one of the main factors in helping to win this war.
I was pointing out that there is a reason why prices remained at a level. Why have prices been stabilized at from $8.31 to $9.16 a hundredweight in this war? The reason is that immediately this war was declared, we entered into an agreement with the British government. We did not wait until farm organizations compelled us to do it; we did not wait until delegations came to Ottawa; we went immediately to Britain. The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) was the delegate of this government to the British isles in the first few weeks of the war; and as a result of the mission he carried on then, a certain price arrangement and quantity arrangement was made with the British government. It was that arrangement which held the price of hogs and bacon up throughout that year and stabilized the price.
The hon. member for Haldimand said that last year the farmers did not know what to
Supply-State oj Agriculture

do because they did not know what the price was or was going to be. The farmers of Canada knew so well what the government had done that they increased the production of hogs in this country to a point which it had never reached before, and more hogs are coming on, the market than ever before. I know that in reply to that he would say, Why did you let it go down twelve cents a hundredweight as against the average of last year, a little less than a dollar a hundredweight or a little less as against the highest price of last year? Why did you let it go down when you were making the second agreement?
There is only one answer I can give to that. The answer is that when we made the first agreement we did not know that Denmark was going to fall, or that Norway or Holland or Belgium or France were going to fall. If we had known, we would not have made an agreement for as high a price as we did for 1940, because we would have known that under the circumstances it would be most difficult for the British government to carry out such an agreement. Britain did not know. Because neither of us knew, one of the best agreements with the best possible price was made. If one questions that, Britain could have bought her pork supplies in the United States all last year on an average of three cents a pound less live weight than she paid for them in Canada. But when Britain had signed on the dotted line, she carried out the agreement. In, spite of the fact that we cabled Britain last June, and cabled again in July, offering to send over additional supplies without suggesting an increased price, even suggesting a decreased price, Britain cabled back that she was going right through with the agreement. And she went through.
When we went back after a year, all the facts being taken into consideration, Britain again entered into an agreement with us, not as good as the one before as to price it is true, but an agreement which took a much greater quantity; and if she had not done so, I do not know what the price of hogs would be in Canada at the present time. If we had had an agreement for only 290 million pounds of bacon for Britain this year and Britain had not taken any more than that, we would not be getting five cents a pound for hogs in Canada now, and everyone who knows anything about the hog trade knows it. But because we have an agreement with Britain, because she realizes the condition of our agriculture, realizing at the same time that neither she nor ourselves can do all for agriculture that ought to be done for it, she has done the best she can, and we have accepted it as the best she can do.

I want to say for the farm population of Canada that, in spite of propaganda put out by some persons who are not farmers and spread across this country, the old gentleman who got up in London, whom the hon. member for Haldimand 'heard, expressed their viewpoint. I am not going to use his language; probably it would not be parliamentary, but the effect was: "I am going to produce all the hogs I can produce, no matter what the price, so long as Britain needs them". That has been the sentiment of the farmers throughout Canada ever since this war started : "We are going to produce hogs; we are going to make them available". In so far as this government is concerned all one has to do in order to know what our position is in relation to hogs, wheat, munitions of war and everything else needed is to read the statement that the Prime Minister put on Hansard yesterday relating to the needs confronting us at the present time in connection with financing this war. Reading that, we shall realize why it is difficult, even for govemr ments, to do the things they wish to do in order to help people over hard places.
I see it is six o'clock and I cannot finish at this time. May I say before moving the adjournment of the debate that I believe, with my friends who have spoken, that farmers are in a difficult position. Prices are not as high as they ought to be in the interests of agriculture. The best the government can do under the circumstances is to look agriculture over from month to month and to search out the branches of agriculture to which the condition I am about to set out relates.
The position taken since the beginning of the war is to the effect that before any branch of agriculture receives assistance because wTe are at war it must be shown (1) that the market which existed for the product of that branch of agriculture has been seriously curtailed by the war; (2) that those engaged in that branch of the industry cannot readily change to any other without lapse of time and unreasonable expense, and (3) that those engaged in that branch of agriculture cannot maintain themselves in agriculture without government assistance. Whenever any branch of agriculture has been found to fit in with that condition, we have attempted to do something about it.
On a later date I hope to have the opportunity of continuing the debate.
On motion of Mr. Gardiner the debate was adjourned.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
